subtitle: Real sources, Zener and transistor regulators, current sources for sensors
takeaways: Every real source has an internal resistance
Op-amp loops make voltages and currents exact
Excite the 1 kΩ sensor with 1 mA, not more

slides.title: Real voltage source
bullets: Terminal voltage drops with load current: V_{L} = V_{0} − R_{i}·I_{L}
Typical R_{i}: AA cell 0.1–0.3 Ω, logic output 20–50 Ω, op-amp output ≪ 1 Ω
Power matching R_{L} = R_{i}: P_{max} = V_{0}^{2}/(4R_{i}), but only 50 % efficiency
Supplies and measurement: voltage matching, R_{L} ≫ R_{i}

falstad.name: real_source
falstad.hint: Move the R_L slider to 1.25 Ω: load power peaks at 4.05 W

slides.notes: Battery pack 4.5 V open, 4.0 V at 10 Ω gives R_i = 1.25 Ω. The operating point is the intersection of source line and load line. Calculation in Exercise 3.1.

slides.title: Current source and source transformation
bullets: Good current source: large internal resistance, R_{i} ≫ R_{L}
Never leave an ideal current source open; real ones have a compliance range
Thevenin ↔ Norton: same V_{0} and I_{0} = V_{0}/R_{i}, same for every load
Equivalent only at the terminals: the power lost inside differs

falstad.name: source_transform
falstad.hint: 10 V/10 kΩ and 1 mA ‖ 10 kΩ both give 3.20 V at 4.7 kΩ

slides.notes: Show both models side by side in Falstad and change the load: the terminal voltages stay identical. Ask the students which internal resistor gets warmer. Exercise 3.2.

slides.title: Zener shunt regulator
bullets: Resistor takes the difference: I_{R} = (V_{in} − V_{Z})/R
Zener takes what the load does not need: I_{Z} = I_{R} − I_{L}
Keep I_{Z} ≥ I_{Z,min} (about 5 mA) in every case
Line regulation ≈ r_{Z}/R, output resistance ≈ r_{Z}; poor efficiency

falstad.name: zener_shunt
falstad.hint: 12 V, 220 Ω, 5.6 V: compare V_out open and with 270 Ω load

slides.notes: The full current flows all the time, even without load. Small-signal model with r_Z is in the section on the shunt regulator (Regulation and ripple). With r_Z = 20 Ω and R = 220 Ω, 1 V input ripple gives about 83 mV output ripple.

slides.title: Design recipe: Zener shunt regulator
steps: Lowest V_{in}, full load: R ≤ (V_{in,min} − V_{Z})/(I_{L,max} + I_{Z,min})
Pick the next smaller E-value (12 V, 5.6 V, 20 mA → 220 Ω)
Highest V_{in}, no load: I_{Z,max} = (V_{in,max} − V_{Z})/R, P_{Z} = V_{Z}·I_{Z,max}
Resistor power: P_{R} = (V_{in,max} − V_{Z})^{2}/R, choose the rating
slides.notes: Two worst cases: one for regulation, one for the Zener's power. Full numbers in Exercise 3.3; at 11 V input the 220 Ω design is just at the edge.

slides.title: Falstad: emitter follower regulator

falstad.name: series_regulator
falstad.hint: Switch R_L between 47 Ω and 470 Ω, watch V_Z hardly move

observe: V_{out} = V_{Z} − V_{BE} ≈ 4.9 V; the Zener only supplies I_{B} = I_{L}/(β+1)
Idle current 6.4 mA instead of 114 mA for an equivalent shunt regulator
Transistor power (V_{in} − V_{out})·I_{L} ≈ 0.74 W: heat sink, no short protection
slides.notes: V_BE drifts with −2 mV/K, so V_out is only accurate to about 0.1 V. Comparison with the shunt regulator in Exercise 3.4.

slides.title: Integrated regulators: 78xx vs LM317

left.head: 78xx fixed
bullets: Dropout ≈ 2 V, LDO types 0.1–0.5 V
Current limit, thermal shutdown

right.head: LM317 adjustable
bullets: R_{1} = 240 Ω sets the minimum load
1.25 V/R_{1} alone: a current source

slides.notes: Put the input and output capacitors close to the pins, or the regulator may oscillate. The LM317 has no ground pin; its quiescent current leaves through the output. Exercise 3.5 designs a 5 V supply and an LED current source.

slides.title: Op-amp voltage source with booster
bullets: Reference + non-inverting amplifier: as accurate as V_{ref} and R_{2}/R_{1}
Loop gain makes R_{out} tiny: mΩ instead of the op-amp's 50 Ω
npn booster inside the loop: op-amp delivers only I_{L}/(β+1)
V_{BE} drops out; op-amp output must reach V_{out} + V_{BE}

falstad.name: opamp_voltage_source
falstad.hint: Slide R_L from 1 kΩ to 20 Ω: V_out stays at 5.000 V

slides.notes: Example: LM4040-2.5 with G = 2 gives 5.000 V from 12 V at up to 100 mA, compared with 4.89–4.95 V for the Zener follower. Point out that the simulation has no current limit; transistor power and SOA limit it in reality (Exercise 3.6).

slides.title: BJT current source
bullets: Emitter follows the base: fixed V_{E} → fixed emitter current
Load sits in the collector; keep V_{CE} ≥ 0.3 V (compliance)
Stiff base: divider current ≥ 10·I_{B}, or a Zener or 2 LEDs
Large V_{E} (≥ 1 V) reduces the −2 mV/K drift of V_{BE}

falstad.name: bjt_current_source
falstad.hint: 1 kΩ and 4.7 kΩ: same 1.02 mA; 15 kΩ saturates (0.71 mA)

slides.notes: Capstone thread: 1 mA for the 1 kΩ sensor from 12 V with 10 kΩ/2.2 kΩ and R_E = 1.5 kΩ. The third load is outside the compliance range, so the current drops. Exercise 3.7.

slides.title: Falstad: current mirror

falstad.name: current_mirror
falstad.hint: Change R_L: I_out stays near I_ref = 1.04 mA

observe: Q1 as a diode sets V_{BE}; Q2 with the same V_{BE} copies the current
Both transistors must match and share the same temperature
slides.notes: Change R_ref to show that it alone sets the output current. Mirrors are everywhere inside ICs, including op-amps and references.

slides.section: Op-Amp Current Sources and Sensor Excitation
slides.title: Op-amp current sources
bullets: Op-amp forces V_{RS} = V_{set}: I = V_{set}/R_{S}, V_{BE} drift drops out
With transistor: base current lost (1 % at β = 100), MOSFET avoids it
Floating sensor in the feedback path: exact current, no terminal at ground
Howland pump for grounded loads: needs well matched resistors
slides.rule: I = V_{set}/R_{S}: as accurate as V_{set} and R_{S}
slides.notes: V_set = 1.00 V, R_S = 1.00 kΩ gives 1 mA; the floating sensor shows VOUT2 = 2.385 V at 1385 Ω. Compliance: V_out must stay inside the op-amp output range. Howland derivation in the script section on op-amp current sources.

slides.section: Op-Amp Current Sources and Sensor Excitation
slides.title: Sensor excitation: why 1 mA?
bullets: Pt1000-like sensor: 1000 Ω at 0 °C, 1385 Ω at 100 °C
Constant current makes V_{sensor} linear in T: 3.85 mV/K at 1 mA
Self-heating: 1.39 mW → about 0.55 K error at 0.4 K/mW
The 1 V offset at 0 °C is removed by a bridge (next chapters)
slides.rule: P = I^{2}·R: half the current, a quarter of the self-heating
slides.notes: This is the capstone thread: the sensor must not carry more than 1 mA. Self-heating depends strongly on mounting (still air vs flowing water). Ratiometric measurement in the chapter on voltage references is often better than a precise current.
